The Nasdaq ASPA Ex Japan™ Index (NQASPAXJP™) led with a gain of 3.8%, extending its year-to-date return to 21.7%, followed by the Nasdaq Emerging Markets™ Index (NQEM™) at 3.1%. The Nasdaq US Large Cap™ Index (NQUSL™) advanced 2.8%, while the Nasdaq Global™ Index (NQGI™) and Nasdaq DM Ex United States™ Index (NQDMXUS™) each gained 2.7%. The average return for this group of indexes was 2.5%. Nasdaq Sector-Specific Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. Two of six Nasdaq Sector-Specific Indexes posted positive returns in August. The PHLX Gold/Silver Sector™ Index (XAU™) led with a gain of 32.4%, making it the top performer across all indexes in the report and lifting its year-to-date return to 19.1%. The KBW Financial Sector Dividend Yield™ Index (KDX™) followed with a gain of 5.8%. Despite slight monthly pullbacks, the KBW Nasdaq Bank™ Index (BKX™) , KBW Regional Banking™ Index (KRX™) , and KBW Premium Yield Equity REIT™ Index (KYX™) retained year-to-date gains of 12.9%, 14.6%, and 17.6%, respectively. The group averaged a gain of 4.9% for the month. Nasdaq Thematic Indexes Source: Nasdaq Global Indexes, Data as of 8/31/2026. All twenty-six Nasdaq Thematic Tech Indexes with reported performance finished August in positive territory, with cloud computing, biotechnology, cybersecurity, and artificial intelligence themes leading the broad rebound. The BVP Nasdaq Emerging Cloud™ Index (EMCLOUD™) was the top performer at 21.8%, followed by the ISE CTA Cloud Computing™ Index (CPQ™) at 15.6% and the Nasdaq Lux Health Tech™ Index (NQHTEC™) at 12.7%. The Nasdaq Biotechnology® Index (NBI®) advanced 10.4%, lifting its year-to-date return to 24.8%. title: From "Export" to "Overseas Revenue": A Share Evidence of China’s Global Expansion
author: Phoebe Wang
description: China’s corporate globalization story has entered a new phase. Exports still matter, but they no longer capture the full picture. As companies expand overseas sales networks and operations, overseas revenue provides a more direct signal of globalization than exports alone.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways China’s globalization is evolving beyond exports. Overseas revenue is becoming a more meaningful indicator of global expansion as Chinese companies build international sales networks and operations, rather than relying solely on exports. Global exposure remains uneven but meaningful. While many companies still have limited international revenue, a growing segment has substantial overseas exposure Companies with higher overseas revenue tend to outperform. Technology companies show the deepest international penetration. A significant portion of overseas revenue in the IT sector comes from firms where international markets account for more than half of total revenue. China’s corporate globalization story has entered a new phase. Exports still matter, but they no longer capture the full picture. As companies expand overseas sales networks and operations, overseas revenue provides a more direct signal of globalization than exports alone. Using A-share disclosures , this blog documents how overseas revenue has broadened across the onshore universe, become more material in aggregate, and diverged meaningfully across industries. While the theme also spans offshore listings, the analysis here focuses on A-shares to quantify how overseas revenue exposure has evolved within the onshore listed universe. Overseas Revenue Expansion Is Broadening and Becoming More Material The “going global” narrative is sometimes framed as a story driven by a small set of exporters. A-share disclosures suggest something broader. More companies are reporting non-zero overseas revenue in annual reports, indicating that overseas revenue exposure is becoming increasingly common across the listed universe. Chart 1 puts that growth in context by showing both the total A-share universe and the subset reporting overseas revenue. From 2015 to 2025, the total coun t rose from 2,808 to 5,470, while companies reporting overseas revenue increased from 1,615 to 3,803, lifting the share from roughly 58% to nearly 70%. This points to overseas revenue becoming a more standard feature of A-share disclosure over time. Chart 1: Number of Globalization Participants Breadth, however, is only part of the picture. The more important question is whether overseas revenue is becoming economically meaningful in aggregate. The revenue mix data ( Chart 2 ) points to a sustained growth differential: over 2015–2025, overseas revenue grew at a +15.17% 10-year CAGR, compared with +8.68% for domestic revenue. That gap has gradually lifted overseas revenue’s share of total revenue from 10% in 2015 to 17% in 2025. The overseas share slipped from 13% in 2019 to 12% in 2020 and remained at 12% in 2021, a pattern that is consistent with the pandemic-era disruption to cross-border demand and logistics. From 2022 onward, overseas revenue resumed its upward trajectory, while domestic revenue has moderated in the most recent years. Chart 2: A-share Companies' Overseas Revenue Grew Faster than Domestic Revenue Aggregate trends can still mask how uneven overseas exposure is across individual companies. A distribution view helps distinguish companies with incidental overseas revenue from those for which overseas markets are central to the business. Chart 3 shows that overseas revenue exposure remains skewed toward the lower end: 2,426 companies fall in the 0%–25% overseas revenue share bucket. Another 1,667 companies report zero overseas revenue. At the other end, a meaningful subset has built deeper overseas footprints, with 755 companies in the 25%–50% bucket and 622 companies with more than 50% of revenue from overseas. Median market capitalization is relatively similar across buckets, clustered in the 6–7 billion CNY range, suggesting the dispersion is not primarily a size effect. Chart 3: Overseas Revenue Share Bucket With breadth, the shift in the revenue mix toward overseas revenue, and the dispersion established, it is natural to ask whether companies with overseas revenue exposure also look different on fundamentals. Overseas Revenue Exposure Aligns with Stronger Growth and Quality Metrics In this section, the data is kept intentionally straightforward. Companies are grouped by overseas revenue share as of year-end 2025, and the comparison focuses on one growth metric, one profitability metric, and one earnings-growth metric. Chart 4a shows a separation between purely domestic companies and those with overseas revenue exposure. Median three-year annualized sales growth is measured over FY2022 to FY2025. Recent sales growth is essentially flat for the zero overseas revenue bucket at 0.14%, then steps higher once overseas revenue appears and continues to rise with greater overseas exposure, reaching 6.25% in the more than 50% bucket. Chart 4a: Sales Growth by Overseas Revenue Share Bucket Profitability shows a similar gradient ( Chart 4b ). Median Return on Equity (ROE) rises from 2.79% in the zero-overseas bucket to 6.61% in the more than 50% bucket. ROE is a simple gauge of how much profit a company generates for each unit of shareholder equity and the upward profile suggests that higher overseas exposure is associated with stronger capital efficiency in this year-end 2025 snapshot. Chart 4b: ROE by Overseas Revenue Share Bucket Chart 4c adds an earnings momentum lens. Median profit growth over FY2022 to FY2025 is negative through the lower and middle buckets, but turns positive at 3.58% in the more than 50% bucket. Read alongside Charts 4a and 4b , the profit-growth distribution suggests that the strongest overseas-exposure cohort is also where earnings growth has been more resilient in recent years. Chart 4c: Profit Growth by Overseas Revenue Share Bucket The year-end 2025 bucket view links deeper overseas exposure with stronger growth, profitability, and earnings momentum. With median outcomes calculated across sizeable buckets and median market caps clustered in a relatively narrow band across buckets ( Chart 3 ), the pattern is unlikely to be driven by a small number of extreme observations or a simple size effect. Overseas Revenue Concentrates in China’s Advantage Industries As overseas revenue becomes more visible in A-shares, two questions matter most: which sectors contribute the bulk of overseas revenue, and where overseas revenue is deepest at the company level. Overseas revenue is not evenly distributed across A-shares; it clusters in sectors where China’s global competitiveness is most visible. Chart 5 makes that concentration intuitive by comparing each sector’s share of total revenue with its share of total overseas revenue. Industrials remains the anchor because it is large in the domestic economy and stays large overseas. The sharper signal is the overweight in Information Technology and Consumer Discretionary: both are 9% of total revenue, yet they account for 19% and 17% of overseas revenue, respectively. This is consistent with the broader narrative of China’s evolving advantage—from pure shipping-volume exports to competitiveness in electronics, digital-enabling hardware, and scalable consumer products and channels, areas where global trade and supply chains have increasingly centered in Asia and where China has deepened its manufacturing and export presence. Financials remains predominantly domestic-facing, representing 13% of total revenue but only a minimal share of overseas revenue. Chart 5: Industry Contribution to Total Revenue vs. Total Overseas Revenue The depth view ( Chart 6 ) separates broad participation from global-first profiles by splitting sector overseas revenue across exposure buckets. Industrials leads in absolute overseas revenue, with contributions spread across buckets, consistent with broad participation at varying overseas intensity. Information Technology shows greater depth, with a meaningful share coming from the more than 50% bucket, indicating overseas markets are central for a sizeable subset of A-share tech names. Consumer Discretionary tilts toward 25%–50%. Materials is more bifurcated, with weight in both 0%–25% and more than 50%. Energy leans heavily toward 25%–50%, consistent with overseas revenue becoming material as globalization scales, even if it is not yet the primary revenue source. Chart 6: Globalization “Depth” by Industry Overall, the year-end 2025 sector view shows Industrials leading in absolute overseas revenue, with deeper globalization most evident in Information Technology and a scaling profile more common in sectors such as Energy. Conclusion Across A-shares, overseas revenue has become more prevalent, more material in the aggregate mix, and more concentrated in sectors where China tends to compete globally. In future blog posts, we will build on these findings and examine how overseas revenue exposure can be framed as an investment theme and why investors may care. title: Nasdaq Advances Always-On Markets and Tokenized Equities Strategy with Agreement to Invest in Payward
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: Nasdaq announced it has agreed to invest in Payward, the parent company of leading global crypto platform Kraken. This collaboration centers on infrastructure supporting tokenized equities, always-on markets, and the convergence of financial systems and decentralized networks.
content: Nasdaq is taking the next step toward a more connected financial system, advancing the infrastructure needed to support the movement of capital, assets, and liquidity across markets. The company announced today that it has agreed to invest $100 million in Payward, the parent company of leading global crypto platform Kraken. This agreement to invest from Nasdaq Ventures will significantly deepen a relationship first announced in March, when Nasdaq announced its plans to launch an equity token design in coordination with Payward that will put public companies at the center of ownership rights, transparency, and governance. Nasdaq Ventures’ agreement to invest in Payward reflects Nasdaq's conviction in Payward's long-term potential and its role in supporting market modernization, further aligning the two companies as they collaborate on infrastructure supporting tokenized equities, always-on markets, and the convergence of financial systems and decentralized networks. "The next era of market evolution will be defined by how efficiently and seamlessly capital and assets move across the financial system with durable, high-integrity liquidity," said Tal Cohen, President, Nasdaq. "Expanding our relationship with Payward reflects our conviction that Kraken can play an important role in building the infrastructure that supports this evolution. Our partnership advances our work on Nasdaq Equity Tokens and helps build a more connected financial system while preserving the trust, transparency and integrity that underpin capital formation." The agreement to invest in Payward follows the August launch of Nasdaq’s Digital Liquidity Networks (DLN) markets business , which aims to bring together liquidity platforms, tokenization capabilities, and fintech solutions serving the digital assets ecosystem. Together, Payward brings Kraken’s crypto-native execution venue and the xStocks infrastructure layer, and Nasdaq contributes wide-ranging expertise, regulated market infrastructure, surveillance technologies, and more. In addition to the ongoing partnership on tokenized equities, the companies announced today that Payward will adopt Nasdaq's market-leading market surveillance technology, to ensure integrity across Payward's full portfolio of trading venues. Driving the Future of Tokenized Equities As boundaries between mainstream and digital markets are converging, and demand for always-on, programmable liquidity is accelerating, Nasdaq is building the infrastructure that will define and enable this convergence. Following this new investment, Nasdaq and Payward will continue to advance their work on building the operational and commercial infrastructure to support the proposed Nasdaq Equity Tokens (NETs) design by connecting it with Payward's xStocks ecosystem. Nasdaq expects to launch NETs in the second quarter of 2027. That work has already established a foundation for how tokenized equities could move across different market environments while maintaining their intended form for the benefit of issuers and investors. Now, the next phase of the collaboration is focused on advancing the distribution, settlement and trading capabilities needed to support broader adoption of tokenized equities, including interoperability between NETs and Payward's xStocks ecosystem CAUTIONARY NOTE REGARDING FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS Information set forth in this communication contains forward-looking statements that involve a number of risks and uncertainties. The LBMA precious metals market between June and August 2026 was defined by a transition from correction to recovery. Early easing, consolidation then a n August recovery. Hormuz and bonds (naturally intertwined) the key driver; bond markets treat intervention with some disdain Rhona O’Connell, StoneX Financial Ltd; 4 th September May 2026 Any views expressed here are of the writer and do not reflect a house view from NASDAQ. Welcome to our monthly round-up of the LBMA OTC trading volumes in gold, silver, platinum and palladium, as recorded on a daily basis by the Association. These are split into spot, swap/forward, options and LoanLeaseDeposit (LLD) and give a flavour of the markets’ activity and how they were influenced by external forces and news items. Due to technical issues plus some holiday leave, this piece looks back at the June-August this year against June-August 2025 All references to COMEX or NYMEX positioning refer to Managed Money, not commercial positions. General introduction: Daily June-August average compared with daily average for the equivalent period in 2025. Source: LBMA Source: LBMA, StoneX Colour coding ranks the metals against each other in each sector June to August was a particularly eventful period for the precious complex, with the intersection of a hawkish new Fed, an interventionist Treasury, a re-escalating Gulf war, and a structurally weak dollar. Gold, silver, platinum and palladium, September 2025 to early September 2026 Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Silver still the outperformer at +159%; Platinum 125%, Gold 124% and palladium, 118% The three key drivers overall included the vicissitudes of the Gulf war, a dollar that was weak against the euro while strong against the yen – although it could be argued that the yen was independently weak - and a virtual tug-of-war developed between Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessen, which is particularly relevant for gold. By the end of the period, the dollar-debasement argument, which had been fading, reasserted itself. After the rally in May, especially in silver, all four metals drifted lower through June and July as the summer doldrums set in and once again some major players were unwilling to take strategic positions. The dollar strengthened in June during the ceasefire in the Gulf but once escalation had resumed the currency entered a downward path that only paused for breath in late August. The metals did rally in late June as the Gulf ceasefire failed, with reciprocal strikes between the US and Iran raising new doubts over the return of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. As we write in early September those doubts have still not been dispelled. In the background it was interesting to see the rising correlation between Brent and the US 10Y yield, but not that surprising since they are both rooted around the Gulf conflict and by definition gold forms part of this matrix also. Growing correlation between Brent and the US 10Y yield since the onset of hostilities Source: Bloomberg, StoneX January 2025 – early September2026 spot volumes, tonnes Gold Silver Source: for all charts above; LBMA, StoneX Platinum Palladium COMEX, NYMEX, positioning to 25 th August 2026 GOLD SILVER PLATINUM PALLADIUM Source: CFTC, StoneX Gold Gold sold off hard in June then spent July trading around $4,100 and occasionally dipping toward $4,000 in one interesting development, gold opened lower on July 13 and fell further despite the US–Iran airstrikes over that weekend, a telling sign that the hawkish-Fed/yield story was overriding the geopolitical safe-haven bid at that point. From a mid-July trough just below$4,000, the metal then staged its best stretch of the year, rallying: by 18% from its mid-July low to an intraday high of $4,696 on August 25 th , its highest since mid-May, before snapping a five-day winning streak late in the month after US inflation data came in above target, then steadying near $4,400–$4,600 into month-end. That mid-August week was gold's best since January, and gold-mining stocks had their hottest five-day run since 2008. Inverted gold and the real two-year yield Source: Bloomberg, StoneX It may seem counter-intuitive that gold prices were rising in the face of continuing increases in bond yields, but this is explained as follows. Yields were rising on inflation and fiscal fears rather than growth; a widening fiscal deficit, inflation persistently above 2% (for 65 months above target as Keviin Warsh noted in his Jackson Hole presentation at end-August), a weaker dollar, and an avalanche of corporate bond issuance to fund AI and data-centre build-outs — which is precisely an environment in which gold can flourish. Second, and probably more significantly, the Treasury Secretary’s efforts to suppress yields via FX intervention (something which almost invariably fails) were seen by the markets as an effort at fiscal dominance and financial repression: an admission that the debt load could no longer tolerate market-clearing rates. Sure enough, by early September 30-year yields were back over 5.2%. The US 5Y-30Y curve; long-term Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Adding to gold’s August rally were soft inflation numbers, but not soft enough for the Fed and Mr Warsh’s Jackson Hole comments were visibly more hawkish than the post-FOMC Press conferences held previously. Trading activity Turnover, M ounces Source: NASDAQ, LBMA As far as market turnover is concerned, the sell-off in early June was in the heaviest volume of the period, with over 30M ounces traded on each of three consecutive days. The rest of June was relatively busy but turnover in July was paltry. After some improvement in early August, the 5 th was particularly heavy as optimism grew over the possibility of Hormuz being reopened and with hedge funds getting on board gold rallied from $4,066 to $4,268, laying the foundations for consolidation in a new range, and latterly for the rally to almost $4,700 at month-end. That rally was in relatively thin conditions until the high-volume sell-off on the 28 th in the wake of Kevin Warsh’s comments. Gold from September 2025 Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Among the OTC derivative sectors, swaps/forwards were sluggish in June until towards month-end when, after falling below the 10-day moving average, forward activity picked up and helped to drive the price to the low for the period ($3,943 intraday). Activity increased in July and on more than one occasion seemed to be related to technical indicators, notably the moving averages. This was mirrored to an extent in the LLD segment, notably in early mid-July where heavy activity around $4,100 suggests that there was some supply-side hedging going through the market as prices failed at this level. As LLD volumes drifted off, the path higher became easier and indeed there was only one LLD trading day in August and that came on the 5th, quelling an initial attempt to clear $4,400. Volumes were high in mid-late July, with prices moving sideways, suggesting good two-way activity. After a busy day early in August, with a failed assault on $4,400, swaps/forwards tailed off. Finally the options market the volume over the period was almost double that of June-August 2025, with a daily average of almost 1.1M ounces. Even so, volumes were sluggish in June and July. The stand-out day, with 4.9M ounces going through was again 5 th August, along with high volumes in spot and swaps/forwards, suggesting that part of that swollen volume was hedging against options exposure. This was on that same day when the market rallied off the 20-day moving average at $4065 to $4,268; i.e. the 5 th when on hopes that Hormuz would reopen. Over the period the ETF gold holdings opened at 4,121t, briefly continued the decline that had started in mid-May, but then turned higher to close Augst at 4,181t, a net year-to-date gain of 156t. CFTC figures show outright Managed money longs rising from 402t to 497t on 25 th August, while outright shorts fluctuated from 54t to 64t the following week, fluctuated around 50t for much of the rest of the period before short covering into 23t in early Augst ; they closed the period higher again, at 47t. Gold and the S&P (log-scales) Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Silver As usual, silver was the highest-beta play on the same macro forces outlined above, and once again it moved violently. After a January record near $121–$122, it had already halved by early summer, opening June at $74 before a two-leg tumble to $56 on the 24 th , and entering a five-week period in a sideways trend between$55 and $63. This set the scene for the August recovery, with silver reaching an intraday high of &1 on the 28 th before, with gold, going into reverse post-Warsh. Gold and silver action, correlation Source: Bloomberg As well as the major factors that drove gold and by association, silver, the latter metal also has its industrial character to address, given that 70% of silver fabrication (ex-investment) is in industrial uses. The June-quarter hawkish Fed hold at 3.50–3.75% and a divided committee hit silver's industrial engine directly, and the gold-silver ratio widened from a May low near 55:1 to about 69:1 by mid-July — a classic sign of silver underperforming gold in a risk-off environment. The same soft-data/weak-dollar cocktail that lifted gold then drove the August rebound, amplified by silver's leverage. The August rally was accompanied, and to some extent driven by, the return of Managed Monay longs (after quite an exodus earlier in the year), rising from 2,822t in mid-July to 3,444t in late August, while shorts were slower to respond, having continued to expand to 1,368t in mid-August (from 941t in mid-July) then contracting to 1,143t in late August. Gold:silver ratio Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Although the US economy is relatively resilient and the onset of AI, vehicle electrification and solar cells will combine to take silver into an expanding pre-investment deficit, in the immediate term these forces are muffled to a degree with the current surplus of solar cells (and a minor threat from copper) while the ebbs and flows of vehicle electrification are a matter of record – although this is more relevant to the PGM than to silver; see below. Turnover Source: NASDAQ Spot volumes were down 39% over the period compared with June-August 2025. With the exception of 5 th August, much mentioned in our gold comments (Hormuz hopes), silver’s spot volume fluctuations were similar to those of gold with high volume in the June retreat (thus making the market less crowded) and then a sluggish period through to mid-July. As prices stabilised spot activity cautiously increased, although volumes in the rally to $70, which was reached on 21 st August, were patchy. On the 21 st , volumes were much livelier. As hedging activity developed (increased volumes in swaps/forwards and options also) and called a halt to the rally. After three successive efforts to clear $70, the market capitulated and the sharp fall to $66 on the 28 th was in heavy spot volume (but not in the derivatives). Derivatives activity was heavy in June in swaps and forwards, which will certainly have been instrumental in the price fall and would to some extent have been self-fulfilling. The LLD segment was 25% down on the 2025 equivalent and here, too , was busiest in the June fall. There was some cautious interest in mid-August when silver was flirting with $65, suggesting some hedging, especially as the price didn’t clear that level at that stage. Finally there was activity at month-end as silver was again on the retreat. Platinum and palladium Platinum was the "cleanest" fundamental story of the four, driven more by physical scarcity than by the dollar. The market is expected to be in deficit for the fourth consecutive year this year, despite expected falls in auto and jewellery demand, while supply is likely to be broadly steady. South Africa accounts for roughly 72% of refined production, and that concentration was the summer's active risk. National primary output fell from about 5.3 million ounces in 2006 to roughly 3.9 million in 2025 and while looking steady this year it is expected to decline again next year. On the demand side, the hydrogen fuel-cell demand, while coming from a very low base, adds a new industrial floor. Palladium trades heavily on autos (80% of demand comes from catalytic converters in gasoline and hybrid vehicles) so it is exposed to two secular headwinds; platinum substitution and the rise of battery-electric vehicles. The June price softness reflected slower automaker procurement, soft electronics demand, caution in the jewellery sector, plus almost non-existent investment, while supply was steady. The July bounce was seasonal restocking rather than scarcity. The one genuine supply-side tail risk remains geopolitical — Russia is the world's largest palladium producer (nickel by-product), followed by South Africa (platinum by-product) so any escalation of sanctions on Russian metal would be the scenario that could override the surplus narrative, much as it did in 2022. This is still up in the air. Turnover Source: NASDAQ Platinum spot turnover was 49% down on the equivalent period of 2025, while options and LLD were both down by ~20%. Swaps/forwards were the only sector in the black, up by 21%. Trading volumes were choppy, with a couple of heavy days trading in spot in the first week as prices came extended a slide from $1,980 ,although this was not mirrored in the OTC derivatives. The sharp fall from $1,906 to $1,772 was one of those days, and Spot volumes dwindled thereafter as prices slid to $1,535 on 1st July. At this point spot and forwards kicked in, in a classic surge in volume in a price reversal and suggesting industrial forward buying, sparking a period of price consolidation, during which the only point of interest was heavy forward activity on the approach to $1,700, which failed, implying continued industrial interest and quite possibly inventory management. Early August saw heavy volumes in spot forwards and options as prices surged from $1,629 to$1,751, stemming from a second day of oil price declines and a weaker dollar (Gulf again), taking all the metals higher and precipitating a change of range. After a period of consolidation the rally to a four-time failed test of $1,900 enjoyed good volumes in everything except options and the reversal saw strong spot activity, suggesting profit taking / stale bull liquidation. Platinum, palladium and the ratio, five-year view Source: Bloomberg, StoneX Palladium prices moved closely in line with platinum over the period, with the correlation between the two not dropping below 0.84, and reaching 0.90 on occasion. Spot trading patterns were not that similar, however, with the early June fall being more of a thin volume slide. There was some intermittent interest in late July in both spot and forwards as the market started to benefit from its prior period of price consolidation, and setting the scene for the sharp jump in early August that had affected all four metals. Forwards were busy in late July on the approach to $1,300, while there was little options activity until mid-August as prices completed a bear move from the failure at $1,400. That failure had itself been accompanied by heavy LLD volume, suggesting some hedging activity. Platinum, palladium and the spread, five-year view Source: Bloomberg, StoneX

title: The Value of Data Becomes Even More Important in an AI-Powered Financial System
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: Nasdaq's latest whitepaper, Unlocking Financial Markets: Understanding the Role of Data in a Digital Economy, examines how data powers modern capital markets and why trusted information has become one of the most important forms of financial infrastructure.
content: The financial industry is entering another period of profound transformation. The first major shift moved markets from crowded trading floors to electronic infrastructure. The next is already underway. Artificial intelligence is reshaping how decisions are made. Trading is becoming increasingly automated. Market participants are preparing for always-on markets, faster settlement cycles, and new forms of digital infrastructure. Together, these developments point toward a future that is faster, more interconnected, and increasingly dependent on data. That reality sits at the center of Nasdaq's latest whitepaper, Unlocking Financial Markets: Understanding the Role of Data in a Digital Economy , which examines how data powers modern capital markets and why trusted information has become one of the most important forms of financial infrastructure. While conversations about financial data often focus on cost, the paper argues that a more important question is value. "Data is the foundation of every modern financial decision," said Brandon Tepper, Senior Vice President and Global Head of Data for Nasdaq's Capital Access Platforms. "As markets become more automated and AI-enabled, the quality and integrity of the data underneath those decisions becomes increasingly important." Building the Financial Data Stack The financial ecosystem relies on a broad range of information sources. At the base is exchange market data, which provides a transparent view of regulated market activity and serves as the foundation for price discovery. Above that layer sits a growing ecosystem of complementary and alternative data products, including indices, analytics, research, news, and other datasets that help firms generate additional insight. This layered structure has expanded dramatically over the past decade as firms seek new ways to analyze markets, manage risk, and uncover opportunities. Global spending on financial market data surpassed $50 billion in 2025, reflecting growing demand for increasingly sophisticated datasets and analytical tools. Yet the paper finds that the value created throughout the broader ecosystem ultimately depends on the quality and integrity of the foundational layer beneath it. Exchange data serves as the common reference point against which other datasets, analytics, and models are built and validated. A useful way to think about the relationship is through infrastructure. New applications, analytics tools, and AI models may represent the visible innovations attracting attention across the industry, but they depend on an underlying foundation that must remain reliable, resilient, and universally trusted. Why AI Raises the Stakes The growing adoption of artificial intelligence is amplifying the importance of high-quality financial data. AI systems can identify patterns, generate predictions, and automate decisions, but they do not independently determine what is true. Their outputs are only as reliable as the data on which they are trained, tested, and governed. As a result, trusted exchange market data plays a critical role as both a training and validation layer for AI-enabled finance. Standardized, transparent, and auditable market information helps ensure that models remain anchored to observable market outcomes rather than incomplete, fragmented, or unverified signals. This becomes increasingly important as firms deploy AI across portfolio management, trading, risk management, surveillance, compliance, and investment research. In more automated environments, errors can be propagated at greater speed and scale, increasing the importance of maintaining trusted sources of market truth. The paper argues that AI is not reducing the importance of exchange data. Instead, it is increasing demand for the trusted reference layer that allows firms to evaluate models, measure performance, and manage risk with confidence. Preparing for an Always-On Future Artificial intelligence is only one part of a broader evolution underway across financial markets. Industry initiatives ranging from extended trading hours and accelerated settlement to the growing use of digital assets and on-chain infrastructure are creating a financial system that operates with greater speed and continuity than ever before. In that environment, trusted data becomes even more essential. Risk systems require accurate information. Automated workflows require reliable inputs. Smart contracts and digital infrastructure still depend on trusted reference prices that connect automated actions to real-world market value. As the financial system becomes more interconnected, the importance of maintaining a transparent, standardized, and continuously available foundation of market data only grows. "The future financial system will undoubtedly introduce new technologies and new capabilities," Tepper said. "But innovation doesn't eliminate the need for trusted information. If anything, it increases the importance of having a shared source of truth that market participants can rely on." The Foundation of Future Innovation Innovation across financial services continues to accelerate. New data products, analytics platforms, AI workflows, and investment tools are creating significant value throughout the industry. But the research suggests that the success of those innovations remains closely linked to the integrity of the underlying market information from which they derive value. As markets move toward a future defined by greater automation, more continuous trading, and increasingly sophisticated technologies, maintaining trusted market data is not simply a market structure consideration. It is fundamental to preserving transparency, confidence, and innovation across the financial system. And in a world increasingly shaped by AI, the value of data may ultimately be measured not by the insights it generates, but by the trust it enables. Read Nasdaq’s Latest Whitepaper Unlocking Financial Markets: Understanding the Role of Data in a Digital Economy Today .

title: What is Driving Free Cash Flow Yield Performance in Japan?
author: Johnny Chen
description: Free cash flow is the cash a company has left after paying for its operations and investments. Free cash flow ETFs first appeared in the United States in 2016 and began expanding into the APAC region in 2023. This study examines whether free cash flow delivers long-term outperformance in the Japanese equity market and investigates the drivers of its returns.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Examines whether free cash flow delivers long-term outperformance in the Japanese equity market and investigates the drivers of its returns. Free cash flow is the cash a company has left after paying for its operations and investments. Free cash flow ETFs first appeared in the United States in 2016 and began expanding into the APAC region in 2023. This study examines whether free cash flow delivers long-term outperformance in the Japanese equity market and investigates the drivers of its returns. The Rise of Free Cash Flow Strategies in APAC The free cash flow strategy gained significant momentum in APAC recently, with total 35 free cash flow ETFs have been launched in China, Hong Kong, Japan and Korea between 1 January 2023 and 30 June 2026. Chart 1 shows that two newly listed free cash flow ETFs in Japan, each with more than one year of performance history, Global X MSCI Japan Cash Flow Kings ETF 234A and Global X S&P 500 Cash Flow Top 100 ETF (356A) , have delivered one-year total returns of 40% and 33%, as of 30 June 2026. Chart 1: The Launch Trend of Free Cash Flow ETFs Note: Past performance is not indicative of future results Source: Morningstar, Nasdaq Product Intelligence Japan Cash Flow ETF 234A invests in the universe of top 500 large and mid-cap Japanese stocks and is constructed by selecting the 50 stocks with the highest free cash flow yield from the universe. We are interested in whether this free cash flow yield strategy can deliver long-term outperformance and what drives its returns. Examining Long-Term Historical Performance and Value Exposure ETF 234A is a newly launched product with limited history, so we use its underlying index of this ETF to represent the long-term performance of free cash flow yield in Japan. TOPIX 500 index is used as market benchmark because the underlying index is also using the top 500 large and mid-cap as universe. Chart 2 shows that since May 2007, the underlying index of this ETF has delivered an annualized total return of 8.6%, while TOPIX 500 has delivered only 2.6%. This suggests that free cash flow yield in Japan not only generated strong one-year performance (40%) but also outperformed the benchmark from 31 May 2007 to 30 June 2026. The price denominator in free cash flow yield (free cash flow per share divided by stock price) from ETF 234A shares the same denominator as value factor (book value divided by stock price) of TOPIX 500 value index. The TOPIX 500 value index has surged since 2023 following the launch of Japan value program which is a Tokyo stock exchange initiative that encourages Japanese companies, particularly those with low share prices relative to their assets to use capital more efficiently, improve profitability, and better reward shareholders. Compared with the TOPIX 500 value Index, the underlying index of ETF 234A has exhibited a similar surge in returns since 2023, as shown in Chart 2. Therefore, we would like to determine whether the returns based on free cash flow yield are driven by the value factor. Chart 2: Japan Cash Flow Kings ETF 234A Index Performance vs Benchmarks Note: Past performance is not indicative of future results Source: Morningstar, Nasdaq Index Research & Development Looking Inside Free Cash Flow Yield 1) A Factor Lens: Value Matters, so Do Quality and Investment Factors We applied Fama-French five factor model, which is a model that explains asset returns using multiple risk factors rather than just the market, on the underlying index of ETF 234A and TOPIX 500. The model result shown in Chart 3 indicates a higher coefficient and statistically significant exposure to the value factor whereas TOPIX 500’s exposure to value is limited. In 2025, the value factor was associated with the underlying index of ETF 234A 1-year 30% return by adding 7.6 points, which is about 25% of the total return. Overall, the model suggests that the underlying index combines large-cap, value with additional tilts toward companies earning strong profits (high quality) and conservative investing. Chart 3: Output of Fama-French 5 Factor Model Source: Fama-French Model, Nasdaq Index Research & Development 2) Separating Cash-Flow Strength from Valuation for Regression Decomposition Given that free cash flow yield uses stock price in the denominator, a natural question is whether high free cash flow yield companies largely overlap with low-valuation names, and therefore exhibit high exposure to the value factor. More importantly, to what extent is the observed performance of the “free cash flow yield” explained by this value exposure? To address this question, we decompose free cash flow yield by expressing it as Free Cash Flow Per Share / Price = Free Cash Flow Per Share / Book Value (free cash flow component) × Book Value / Price (value component). We then applied the return decomposition framework below to regress the daily returns of the high free cash flow yield portfolio on the TOPIX 500 market return, the free cash flow‑to‑book value return premium, and the book value-to-price premium. This approach allows us to separate the return contributions from the overall market, the free cash flow component, and the value component. Note: The high free cash flow yield portfolio on the left hand side was constructed by selecting the top 250 high free cash flow yield stocks from the top 500 large‑ and mid‑cap universe in Japan. The return premium on the right hand side were constructed using the same methodology as the high free cash flow yield portfolio. The regression results indicate that the high free cash flow yield portfolio’s returns may be driven by market, while both free cash flow‑to‑book value and book value-to-price provide additional independent explanatory power with t-stat 9.57 and 8.93 respectively. Both the free cash flow‑to‑book value and book value-to-price premiums are statistically significant (at the 1% level), not just one. This shows that the free cash flow‑to‑book value component contributes to returns independently of value, beyond the shared price denominator. 3) Interaction Between Free Cash Flow-to-Book and Value Component After showing that both free cash flow‑to‑book value and book‑to‑price are important in explaining returns, the next step is to see whether they interact with each other. In other words, do companies with high free cash flow‑to‑book value behave like traditional value stocks (high book value‑to‑price), or are they different? Looking at the TOPIX 500, if we divide the 500 stocks into high and low groups based on their free cash flow component and value component separately, only one-third of the high free cash flow-to-book stocks also belong to high value group, which indicates that free cash flow and value are capturing different names from the universe. Chart 4 shows the backtested relative performance of each metric, constructed as the high-metric group index divided by the low-metric group. The free cash flow yield (Top 500 FCF/P) tracks the free cash flow component (Top 500 FCF/B) closely, both delivering steady gains. The value component (Top 500 B/P) follows a different path. It led from 2021 to early 2026 but gave back much of that gain over the past four months and saw larger drawdowns throughout. In short, free cash flow yield behaves more like the free cash flow component than like value. Chart 4: Free Cash Flow‑to‑Book Value and Book Value-to-Price Return Premium Note: Past performance is not indicative of future results Source: Morningstar, Nasdaq Index Research & Development Conclusion Because free cash flow yield puts price in the denominator, high free cash flow yield is easily linked to low valuation. But our factor attribution and regression analysis show the free cash flow component has explanatory power beyond value. Furthermore, when decomposing free cash flow yield into its free cash flow and value components, we found that not only is the constituent overlap between the high free cash flow component group and the value group relatively low, but the two groups have also exhibited distinct return patterns. Compared with the existing free cash flow yield methodology used by ETF 234A, the free cash flow component (FCF/B) has demonstrated a steady upward trend over the period from May 2007 through June 2026. Beyond answering the value question, this points to a further possibility worth exploring: FCF/B on its own may be a viable building block for a free cash flow strategy in Japan. title: Chartstopper: September 4, 2026
author: Michael Normyle
description: The two big themes this week were the rate path for the Federal Reserve and the Iran conflict.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways Fed rate path in focus as Waller signals patience August jobs report blows past expectations, lifting hike odds Iran conflict pushes oil back above $90 AVGO caps a blockbuster earnings season Markets finish flat as inflation concerns offset strong earnings This Week The two big themes this week were the rate path for the Federal Reserve and the Iran conflict. For the Fed, there were two notable developments: Fed Governor Chris Waller said he was open to leaving rates unchanged if recent disinflation continues, or, as he put it, “to paraphrase John Lennon… give disinflation a chance.” The economy added 162,000 jobs in August, supporting Chair Kevin Warsh’s view last Friday that inflation is the Fed’s focus . That job gain was nearly triple expectations for 55,000 jobs added, and the previous two months were revised up, flipping July’s job change into positive territory. So, in the last week, market expectations for Fed hikes this year have increased to nearly 40 basis points (bp) from under 30bp. Of course, the Iran conflict isn’t doing the Fed any favors on the inflation front. In the last week, U.S. oil prices are up over $5 to move back above $90 per barrel – near three-month highs. That’s because hopes for any kind of near-term ceasefire seem increasingly remote after the U.S. and Iran continued to exchange strikes and more oil tankers were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz. There were also reports that the Trump administration would not accept a return to the expired Memorandum of Understanding and would require an agreement covering both the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear program. Elsewhere, second-quarter earnings season wrapped up with mega-cap AVGO beating earnings estimates with nearly 100% per annum (p.a.) growth, helping the Nasdaq-100® finish the quarter with almost 80% p.a. earnings growth. Despite the (very) strong earnings growth, concerns about inflation and rate hikes weighed on markets with the Nasdaq-100® finishing the week flat, while 10-year Treasury yields are up about 5bp to 4.8%. title: How the Nasdaq Foundation is Supporting Rural Founders to Build with AI
author: Nasdaq Newsroom
description: This spring, a cohort of rural founders set to work learning and experimenting how to apply artificial intelligence to their entrepreneurial ideas, supported by Nasdaq.
content: This spring, a cohort of rural founders set to work learning and experimenting how to apply artificial intelligence to their entrepreneurial ideas. They convened at the Center on Rural Innovation’s AI Forward Studio , a unique hands-on program funded by the Nasdaq Foundation. The program combined learning with weekly check-ins, mentorship, and a peer community – meeting every founder where they were, whether they had never written a line of code or were ready to push past no-code tools entirely. “With Nasdaq Foundation’s support, the Center on Rural Innovation launched AI Forward Studio, a free, 12-week hands-on learning program that brought together 22 rural startups, which included the founders and their teams,” said Diego Rubio, Senior Program Manager for Entrepreneurship Ecosystems at the Center on Rural Innovation. “This unique program gave entrepreneurs the space and support to experiment with AI tools, access technical guidance and mentorship, and connect with peers while applying AI directly to their startups.” The AI Forward Studio was designed to turn that learning into tangible outcomes, Rubio explained, including reaching more customers, securing funding, and building valuable connections. For the Nasdaq Foundation, the program instantly made sense to fund. “When the Center on Rural Innovation applied for a grant from the Nasdaq Foundation to hold their AI Forward Studio, we immediately recognized what a great idea it was,” said Jailan Griffiths, President of the Nasdaq Foundation and Head of Purpose at Nasdaq. “AI is integral to Nasdaq’s strategy and is quickly shaping tomorrow's economy – so a program that combines that with building the future of rural businesses was a really attractive proposal and ticked so many boxes for us when it came our way.” Griffiths pointed to recent research from the Nasdaq Economic Institute that found AI is enabling more entrepreneurship because of decreased financial barriers to building out the initial products and operations of a company. “The AI economy is taking shape in real time, and it is changing who can start a business, how fast can they scale, and what do they need to get started; and the AI Forward Studio makes sure that rural founders are playing a part in that reshaping,” she said. “The founders who get access to the AI tools letting them do more with less are the ones who are going to help author what comes next, and that offers a unique opportunity to support and revitalize rural economies.” Griffiths explained that the foundation, through its Economic Opportunity Grant Program, targets five areas of impact: Empowering individuals through financial literacy Supporting both new and established ventures by improving access to capital Building a new generation shaping the financial markets by cultivating investor identity Enabling employee and community ownership Strengthening economies and opportunities through regional revitalization and rural wealth building Each of those interconnected pillars, she said, ultimately comes back to Nasdaq’s purpose as an organization. “Our purpose is to empower economic opportunity, and that flows through everything that Nasdaq does as an organization – from our business strategy to our product development, the way we engage our clients, and how we run our markets,” Griffiths said. “And it also flows straight through to the Nasdaq Foundation as well – and our grant program explicitly aims to expand access and create opportunity throughout the economy.” The AI Forward Studio, she noted, fit squarely into the “access to capital” and “regional revitalization and rural wealth building” categories by preparing rural businesses for investment readiness. In fact, Griffiths said, many of the founders who participated in the program are not only driven by the goal of growing their own businesses, but also see rural entrepreneurship as an opportunity to help bring their communities along in their success – not just through job creation, but also through sharing skills that will ready the workforce for the future. For the founders participating in the program, the studio also offered a unique opportunity to rapidly move their business ideas forward. "One thing that's been especially valuable about AI Forward Studio has been the speed to which we can iterate and bring forward our software ideas to a viable alpha stage ready for investor review,” said Jason Vanest, the founder of Brattleboro, Vermont-based Logic Building Systems. Van Nest joined the studio with a software concept in mind, and his team successfully built an initial working prototype within days. Similar experiences occurred throughout the studio’s different entrepreneurial endeavors. “Our biggest takeaway from this program was that rural founders are eager to use AI and can move quickly when they have the right tools, guidance, and space to experiment,” Rubio said. “We saw founders turn ideas into working prototypes, build minimum viable products, win funding, and approach investors with real results.” He added that AI tools will clearly continue to evolve, but “the most valuable outcome was giving founders the confidence, fluency, and judgment to keep experimenting, adapting, and creating long after the program ends.”

title: Biweekly Investment Insights: When hawks fly, stay grounded in the fundamentals
author: Yanni Angelakos
description: Markets have turned more cautious following a hawkish Fed message, rising Treasury yields, and trade tensions. While higher rates may pressure equities near term, earnings expectations remain the stronger driver of Nasdaq-100 performance.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Macro & micro square off (again) as investors move past Q2 earnings season Fed Chair Warsh delivered a hawkish speech at Jackson Hole focused on battling inflation Despite government intervention, Treasury yields have rerated higher U.S. corporate earnings strength & credit spreads still point to a constructive backdrop Biweekly Charts in Focus: Rising Treasury yields can dampen market sentiment, but next 12-month consensus EPS have a stronger historical relationship with equity index returns Source: Bloomberg. As of August 31, 2026, monthly basis. Source: Bloomberg. As of August 31, 2026, monthly basis. Summary The end of a strong Q2 earnings season coincided with August NFPs that were notably above estimates and a decisively hawkish message from Federal Reserve Chair Warsh at the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium on August 28 th : “Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do. That’s our job.” After the recent downshift in the market pricing of Fed rate hike expectations through 2026, they have reset higher as have Treasury yields. Higher Treasury yields typically impact equities via a higher risk-free rate which can reduce the present value of future cash flows and compress equity valuations, all else being equal. They can also tighten financial conditions which dampens risk appetite. However, per our Biweekly Charts in Focus, over the past 20 years, annual changes in Treasury 10-year yields cannot effectively predict YoY changes to the Nasdaq-100. It is the fundamentals such as earnings expectations—measured here by the annual change in Nasdaq-100 NTM consensus EPS—which historically have had greater explanatory power in terms of equity index returns. The markets and the economy have lived with higher rates in the past, and the Treasury 10-year yield matches up directionally with U.S. nominal GDP growth since 1980. As we’ve discussed before , it is not just the rise in rates but it is also why rates are rising which is important. Our decomposition model of nominal Treasury 10-year yield changes YTD continues to point to it being overwhelmingly driven by the change in real rates as a byproduct of Fed policy repricing amidst a resilient U.S. economy. Against this backdrop and amidst shifting equity market returns, corporate earnings and revenue estimates remain solid over the next few quarters. But we are watching to see if lower expectations develop into mid-2027. The strong corporate earnings construct is also reflected in U.S. corporate credit spreads which are hovering near 20-year tights. In the very near-term, as the markets push into what has historically been the weakest month for U.S. equity returns (September), equities could remain unsettled amidst the higher rates backdrop, AI capex questions, and ahead of key macro data points that will further inform the September 16 th Fed meeting. Details Hawkish Warsh commentary & higher Treasury yields Fed Chair Warsh’s speech at Jackson Hole was more in-line with the recent tilt of the FOMC in terms of looking to combat inflation sooner than later. Despite better-than-expected PCE and CPI readings recently, he stressed that “they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.” He also noted that “on balance, I would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive.” Warsh’s latest comments and stronger August NFPs of 162,000 (above consensus of 55,000), along with the two prior months revised higher by a net of 55,000 jobs, sent another reverberation through the market pricing of Fed rate hike expectations. We admit that we show Figure 3 frequently. While it speaks to the evolving market narrative, it is also a reminder that it is important for investors to remain strategically disciplined, and to focus on the health of corporate fundamentals as well as the structural growth stories amidst the macro volatility [ 1 ] . The combination of a broadly resilient U.S. economy, sticky inflation trends and resurgent energy prices, ongoing U.S. fiscal concerns, the market navigating an evolving Fed communications strategy, and the battle for capital globally between governments and AI-related corporate debt (Goldman Sachs estimates nearly $500 billion of AI-related corporate debt issuance in 2026 YTD), has pushed the long-end of the yield curve higher. Figure 3: Number of 25bp hikes priced in by Fed meeting has round-tripped last 3 weeks Source: Bloomberg Treasury Secretary Bessent announced the long-end liquidity buyback program will at least double, raising the per-operation cap from $2 billion to at least $4 billion for 10-, 20-, and 30-year debt effective September 9 th , with the Treasury General Account potentially tapped to fund the operations rather than issuing additional front-end bills. However, 10-year yields are now higher by more than 10 basis points from when Secretary Bessent announced these measures on August 19 th . So, is the Treasury 10-year yield at its highest since January 2025 out of sync with the fundamentals? With nominal U.S. GDP running at 6.6% YoY, as Figure 4 shows, a 10-year yield of around 4.75% does not seem out of bounds (all else being equal given the various dynamics at play such as term premium, inflation dynamics, etc.). A lender extending 10-year credit to the U.S. government would expect, at minimum, to be compensated for the opportunity cost of capital—which is roughly what the economy can generate in nominal terms. Figure 4: Treasury 10-year yields track directionally with U.S. nominal GDP Source: Bloomberg Shifting equity returns & flows Taking a step back, while macro clouds have gathered (again), we continue to note the broadening of equity returns beneath the index levels. As a proxy for the growth versus value trade, as well as for AI enablers versus AI adopters, Figure 5 shows the massive outperformance of semis relative to banks on a 6-month rolling basis—a +4.1 standard deviation move versus the 10-year average as of mid-June 2026. However, banks recovered on a relative basis on the back of strong earnings and a broadly resilient U.S. economy while semis sold off notably in July (SOX was -20.6%, its largest monthly decline since December 2002). This reversal in sentiment can also be seen through the lens of retail flows across baskets of semiconductor and bank names via Nasdaq Data Link’s U.S. Retail Equities Flow (UREF) dataset. Figure 6 shows the difference in retail buying of semi and bank stocks. Based on UREF data, retail investors began to favor semis relative to banks beginning in December 2023, with this net buying activity peaking in May 2025. Semi retail net buying activity continued to be net positive until July 2026 after which it has turned net negative amidst the sell-off in semis—further illustrating the shift in sentiment and speaking to the recent market rotation. Figure 5: Reversal in semis vs. banks speaks to the broadening of equity returns Figure 6: Mirrored reversal in semi vs. bank net dollar retail flows Source: Bloomberg. As of August 28, 2026. Source: Nasdaq Data Link . As of August 28, 2026. Includes semiconductors, semiconductor equipment and materials, and diversified and regional banks. Dollar volumes shown in “current day” dollars, deflated by the change in total U.S.-listed stock market capitalization to facilitate long-horizon comparisons. Following the iShares MSCI U.S. Momentum ETF (MTUM) returning a staggering 42.9% in Q2 2026—its largest quarterly return on record going back to 2013—per Figure 7, it has notably retrenched relative to the iShares MSCI U.S. Quality ETF (QUAL). While still higher by 20% YTD as of August 31 st , with MTUM’s top four names being AI stalwarts and comprising 20% of the ETF’s weight, and semis accounting for over 35% of the ETF’s weight, MTUM has sold off as investors have rotated into other parts of the market. When the quality factor outperforms, it can be a signal that investors are favoring corporate characteristics such as earnings durability, balance sheet strength, and low financial leverage amidst a volatile macro backdrop, Fed policy uncertainties, questions around AI capex, and an elevated financing environment. Figure 7: Momentum has sold off while the quality factor has come more into favor Source: Bloomberg. As of August 28, 2026. Solid corporate fundamentals, but watching for slowing earnings growth expectations Market gyrations are typically important to monitor for investor read throughs. But when investing for the longer-term, corporate fundamentals tend to be the driver of equity returns and broader risk taking. Following the outsized, AI-driven S&P 500 earnings growth in Q2, EPS growth is expected to remain very strong over the next three quarters—even if moderating from lofty levels (Figure 8). Likewise, S&P 500 sales growth is expected to be at least 10% YoY through Q1 2027. However, as the base effect becomes more challenging heading into mid-2027, these growth expectations bear watching in terms of a more material slowdown—albeit from very elevated levels. Another key proxy for the health of U.S. corporate fundamentals are credit spreads. The strong corporate earnings dynamics are also expressed via fixed income markets with both high yield and investment grade credit spreads hovering near their tightest levels since mid-2007 (Figure 9). It is worth noting that tech issuance is making up greater portions of the credit market—40% of 15-year-plus investment grade issuance in 2026 has come from companies related to the AI buildout, per Goldman Sachs. Across the pond, the hyperscalers alone comprised over 5% of Euro-denominated IG issuance YTD, per the ECB. On top of the angst around higher rates and AI capex questions, September tends to be the weakest month for U.S. equities historically with an average return of -0.2% since 1945 (Figure 10). The higher rates dynamic coupled with the historical volatility ahead of November U.S. mid-term elections (per our prior report ), could keep market sentiment fragile in the very near-term. title: Second-Quarter Earnings Show Breadth
author: Phil Mackintosh
description: 2026's market rally isn't just AI. Q2 earnings growth hit multi-year highs across chips, large caps, and beyond — with P/E multiples actually falling.
content: AI Summary Summarize with Google AI Summarize in ChatGPT Explore with Perplexity Analyze with Claude Get Insights via Grok Key Takeaways AI Trade Rotation: From hyperscalers to chipmakers in the "picks-and-shovels" trade. SOX™ Fundamentals-Driven Rally: ~60% YTD price gain matched by ~60% earnings growth; 75% more projected next year. Nasdaq-100® Earnings Breadth at 4½-Year High: Over half of constituents with 20%+ growth; Q2 earnings near 80% p.a. — strongest since 2010. Large-Cap Valuations Compressing: Forward earnings outpacing price returns; P/E multiples falling despite record highs. Broader Than AI: Mid/small caps pricing in recovery on rate cuts, cooling wages, and tax tailwinds — strength extends well beyond chips. For markets, the artificial intelligence (AI) trade has been the dominant theme for the last couple of years. But it has shifted this year. Last year's story was about the AI hyperscalers – the handful of mega-cap tech companies spending hundreds of billions to build out AI infrastructure. This year, investors have rotated one step back in the supply chain. The "picks-and-shovels" trade is here, and chipmakers are the biggest beneficiaries. One constant, though, is that there’s been strong earnings growth underpinning this AI trade all along. In fact, the earnings strength we’ve seen in the AI hyperscalers and now chipmakers is accompanied by a broad-based strength across U.S. equities this year and in second-quarter earnings. SOX semis index sees price return and earnings moving in lockstep A key measure of chips stocks is the PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index™ (SOX™), and it’s up about 60% year-to-date. That's a remarkable number. But what's more remarkable is what's behind it. SOX™ earnings are up over 60% this year (in just two quarters) – roughly in line with the price gain. And analysts project another 75% earnings growth by the end of next year. So, it’s been fundamentals driving this rally. Chart 1: Chips stocks’ prices and earnings are both up about 60% this year That’s also the key difference from the dot-com bubble. In 1999, valuations were running well ahead of earnings (if there were any earnings). Now, earnings are supporting price gains. In fact, for many sectors this year (including the SOX™), price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples are actually falling as earnings rise faster than stock prices (Chart 3). Nasdaq-100® earnings breadth is at 4½-year high The attention on the chipmaker rally can obscure something worth highlighting — earnings growth in 2026 has become remarkably broad-based. As of the second quarter, over half of all Nasdaq-100® companies reported earnings growth of at least 20% per annum (p.a.). More than four in five reported positive earnings growth. Both are the highest readings since the fourth quarter of 2021 — going back to the early post-Covid recovery. This breadth has helped push Nasdaq-100® earnings growth near 80% p.a. in the second quarter — its strongest earnings growth since 2010, when companies were recovering from the depths of the global financial crisis. Chart 2: Earnings breadth pushing Nasdaq-100® near 80% p.a. earnings growth Of course, there are some special circumstances here, with earnings boosted by tariff refunds and marking to market holdings in private companies like Anthropic. Still, even without these factors, large-cap earnings are robust. For large caps, earnings are outpacing returns With the SOX™, the Nasdaq-100® and the S&P 500 all near record highs, it's natural to wonder whether valuations are getting stretched. The data says no — in fact, they’re compressing. Across the major large-cap indexes, forward earnings growth has been outpacing price returns year-to-date. That means P/E multiples are falling as earnings climb faster than prices. That's true for the hyperscalers, the chipmakers, and the broader Nasdaq-100® and S&P 500. Chart 3: Large-cap earnings outpacing price growth, compressing PEs For mid and small caps, markets are betting on stronger earnings The valuation story is a little different once you move down the market cap spectrum. For mid caps (S&P 400), P/E multiples are flat year-to-date. For small caps (S&P 600), they're up nearly 5%. In other words, prices have been rising in line with or a bit faster than earnings for these groups – at most, a modest degree of multiple expansion. Multiple expansion, when it's modest, often reflects investors pricing in expected earnings improvement rather than paying for growth that has already arrived. And there are good reasons to expect it. Earlier rate cuts are feeding through to smaller companies, which carry more floating-rate debt than their large-cap peers. Wage growth is cooling. Tax tailwinds are flowing through to corporate earnings. Market’s strength goes well beyond chips and AI So, what do we make of all this? The SOX™ is the latest headline act and the earnings behind it are real. But framing 2026 as purely a chips or AI story misses most of the picture. The broader market resilience reflects macro tailwinds doing serious work. That combination has lifted a far wider set of companies than the headlines suggest.

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to lift block on U.S. Postal Service mail-in ballots rule
description: Justice Brett Kavanaugh said that applying the U.S. Postal Service rule in the 2026 midterm elections "would be arbitrary and capricious."
content: The U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, June 29, 2026. Graeme Sloan | Bloomberg | Getty Images The Supreme Court on Monday night rejected a request by the Trump administration to lift a judicial block on a controversial U.S. Postal Service rule that critics feared would make it more difficult to vote by mail in the upcoming midterm elections . In an unsigned order, the Supreme Court said the administration "is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the" preliminary injunction issued by a federal court judge in Boston preventing the USPS rule from being used in November's elections nationwide. The decision comes less than two months before Election Day for contests that will determine which political party controls each chamber of Congress. President Donald Trump 's fellow Republicans hold slim majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump appointee, concurred with the ruling in a statement that said, "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority." "But applying the rule in the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections," Kavanaugh added. "For that reason, I concur in the denial of the application for stay." Two of Kavanaugh's fellow conservatives on the nine-justice court, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, dissented from the decision to reject a stay of the injunction against the Postal Service rule, which was issued in late August. That rule, which implemented an executive order issued by Trump in March, established new standards for ballot envelopes and required states to create lists of voters who were eligible to obtain mail ballots. Monday's decision by the Supreme Court only prevents the Postal Service's rule from being used in November's elections. It is possible that the court will allow the rule to be used in future elections. Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Analysis: Hot inflation data sets up a Fed rate hike. What happens if Warsh wavers Hassett kept up to $5 million Coinbase stake as Trump reshaped crypto policy Trump's energy holdings have surged as the Iran war moved oil markets Alito, in his written dissent, said that some of the plaintiffs who had sued to challenge the Postal Service's rule lacked legal standing to do so, "while the remainder are pursuing a claim that this Court has recently called a 'Hail Mary pass' that 'rarely succeeds.'" "The Government has a strong interest in enforcing the rule, and implementing it will also 'enhance the visibility of Federal Ballot Mail' in order to better detect election fraud," Alito wrote. "On the other side of the balance, the plaintiff States invoke the practical effects of implementing the rule close to the midterm elections. I take that problem very seriously, but it is not enough to convince me to deny the application." Celina Stewart, CEO of the League of Women Voters, one of the plaintiffs in the case, said in a statement , "Today, the Supreme Court refused to allow the federal government to throw our elections into chaos just weeks before Election Day." "The Postal Service exists to deliver Americans' mail — not to rewrite election rules, demand voters' personal information, or decide which ballots make it through the system," Stewart said. "This was an extraordinary attempt to interfere with voting in all 50 states, and voters should never have been put in this position. Voters should never be caught in the middle of a political power warfare." New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was part of the coalition suing to block the rule, said in a statement, "I am truly relieved the Court granted this reprieve." "Voters should never have to wonder whether a ballot they legally cast will be counted because the federal government suddenly changed the rules," James said. "We will keep fighting to make sure every eligible ballot is counted come November. Now, I encourage all eligible Americans to get out and vote – and vote early." title: Mitch McConnell returns to Senate after three-month health absence
description: The 84-year-old Kentucky Republican is back in Washington after a fall, hospitalization, pneumonia and weeks of rehabilitation kept him away from the Senate.
content: U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) speaks to the press as he arrives for a vote at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 14, 2026 in Washington, D.C. Finn Gomez | Getty Images Sen. Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., returned to the Capitol on Monday after a three-month absence following a fall that left him hospitalized and out of public view for 92 days. McConnell said he has assured Senate Majority Leader John Thune that he will "do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me." "Today, I'll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June," McConnell said in a statement. "I'm really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues." The appearance is the first time the 84-year-old former Senate Republican leader had been seen publicly since he was hospitalized June 14, ending months of questions about his condition and whether he would be able to return before his final term expires in January . McConnell had not cast a Senate vote since June 11 and missed dozens of votes during his absence. His return comes as senators reconvene Monday following a five-week summer recess. McConnell, considered a master of legislative rules , was hospitalized after falling at his Washington home on June 14. He later said the fall briefly knocked him unconscious but that doctors determined he had not suffered a heart attack, stroke or concussion and had not broken any bones. He subsequently developed what his office described as a mild case of pneumonia. After nearly a month in the hospital, McConnell said in July that he had been transferred to a rehabilitation center . He remained there for more than three weeks before announcing Aug. 6 that he had been discharged and would continue an " intensive regimen of physical therapy " from home. But McConnell's prolonged absence from public view fueled mounting scrutiny over his health. His office released written statements and two photos of McConnell during his recovery, including one showing him alongside his wife , former Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao, holding a newspaper. Until Monday, however, no public video or audio of the senator had been released since his hospitalization. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat, escalated that pressure in July, calling on McConnell to " provide proof of your capacity to serve, or resign ." Beshear suggested McConnell could release a short video or speak with a Kentucky television or radio station and asked Senate Majority Leader John Thune to investigate his condition if he failed to demonstrate that he could continue serving. McConnell, who arrived to the Senate in a wheelchair, acknowledged Monday that his recovery has been "a long and often frustrating process" and said the lingering effects of childhood polio have complicated it. He said he is "still not quite back to 100%" and will continue physical therapy on the advice of his doctors. McConnell's return also restores another available vote for Republicans, who hold a 53-47 Senate majority. The Kentucky Republican is serving the final months of a Senate career that has spanned more than four decades. McConnell announced last year that he would not seek an eighth term, setting up his departure from the Senate in January. His tenure has helped reshape the federal judiciary and the modern Republican Party . As majority leader, McConnell blocked consideration of President Barack Obama's Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland in 2016 and later oversaw the confirmation of all three of President Donald Trump's first-term Supreme Court nominees.
